solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: See what is being said?

parts.note: the surface wants 'understand', as in 'I see'; the setter means using your eyes
the words spoken, which here are watched rather than heard

explanation.walkthrough: 'See what is being said?' sounds like 'do you understand?', but taken literally it describes reading words off someone's lips.
explanation.definitionFit: To lip-read is to follow speech by watching the speaker's mouth, literally seeing the words.

clue.text: Animal catcher employed by professional association

indicators.note: the answer is at work inside the following words

explanation.surface: A trade body takes on someone to round up stray animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Employed by' reads as a job offer, but it means the answer sits inside the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a looped rope used to catch cattle and horses.

clue.text: Great office of strait-laced English clergyman

explanation.surface: A stuffy English vicar holds some grand position in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the prime minister's post is one of the four Great Offices of State, alongside Chancellor, Foreign Secretary and Home Secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Prime minister is the highest of the Great Offices of State in British government.

clue.text: Additional cast member having little to do

definitions.meaning: more than the usual amount, over and above

definitions.text: cast member having little to do
definitions.meaning: a background performer in a film crowd scene, with no lines

explanation.surface: A spare actor is hired who has hardly any part.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses run together so smoothly that the clue reads as one description of a bit-part player.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is something additional, and also a background performer in a film.

clue.text: Stubborn person put on small island

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on
a key (or cay) is a small low island, as in the Florida Keys

explanation.surface: An obstinate man gets marooned on a tiny island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' looks like 'marooned', but it means dressing: DON.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative use: the animal is proverbially obstinate, so the name is thrown at a mulish human.

clue.text: Bring back drink fit for a king

indicators.note: bringing the word back reads it right to left

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a drink to be brought back that would suit royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring back drink' reads like ordering another round, but it tells you to write LAGER backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Regal means royal, befitting a king.

clue.text: Refuse to criticise

definitions.meaning: the noun, stressed REF-use: household waste
a British verb for dismissing something as worthless

explanation.surface: Someone declines to find fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' wants to be the verb, declining; it is the noun, household waste.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the noun for waste, a plain synonym of the noun refuse, and the informal British verb meaning to pour scorn on.

clue.text: Pleasure beginning to gain approval

indicators.note: the beginning of 'gain' is its first letter

explanation.surface: The joy of starting to win people's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to gain approval' reads as one phrase about winning support; split it after 'gain' to find G and the formal word for approval.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word names the satisfaction felt when a wish is met, which is a kind of pleasure.

clue.text: Boisterous young woman jetted all over naked

indicators.note: Turned over, the letters are read the other way round.
Stripped of its outer covering, the phrase loses its first and last letters.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across the words, read backwards

explanation.surface: A rowdy girl has flown all over the world without her clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All over' looks like a single phrase meaning everywhere; 'over' turns the letters round. A ladette is British slang for a young woman who drinks and behaves as rowdily as the lads.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladette is a young woman who behaves in a loud, hard-drinking, laddish way.

clue.text: What goes round room, bypassing senior management?

definitions.meaning: the strip of wood running round the base of a room's walls

explanation.surface: Office gossip that circulates while the bosses are kept out of the loop.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical: read the answer as a verb phrase, going around the company board. A skirting board is the wooden strip where wall meets floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A skirting board runs round the bottom of a room's walls.

clue.text: Work with case in theatre

parts.note: opera is Latin for 'works', and an opera is a musical work

indicators.note: a case is an outer shell, so the case in a word is its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A surgeon deals with a patient in the operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two pieces. In hospital talk a case is a patient and the theatre is where surgery happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes a surgeon at work on a patient in the operating theatre, which is exactly what operating means.

clue.text: Papers I returned to fool

indicators.note: sent back, so read right to left

explanation.surface: Someone sent the documents back to a clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned to' reads as sending papers back to someone; it is TO that comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name a stupid person, and both work as insults.

clue.text: In GCHQ, briefly shed light on computer problem

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other
cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: GCHQ losing its last letter Q

explanation.surface: Inside Britain's spy agency, someone briefly explains a bug in the system.
explanation.walkthrough: LIT goes inside G_CH. GCHQ is Britain's government communications and signals intelligence agency.
explanation.definitionFit: A glitch is a sudden malfunction, especially in a computer.

clue.text: Broadcast enraged eminent individual

indicators.note: scattered, like seed sown by hand

explanation.surface: A furious bigwig goes on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' reads as a TV or radio verb, but its older sense is scattering seed, which is why it mixes letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandee is a person of high rank or eminence, originally a Spanish nobleman.

clue.text: Calm surrounds every other part of unitary authority

indicators.note: one word goes round the other
every other means one in two, so only alternate letters of the next word are kept, here the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: Peace settles across a local council area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unitary authority' looks like a single term, a type of English local council; split it, and 'authority' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having authority over people means having the power to direct them.

clue.text: Exquisite selection

definitions.meaning: an adjective: of the finest quality, as a butcher's best cuts
a noun: the range to pick from, or the pick made

explanation.surface: A superb range on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: One word is the adjective, the other the noun, and both are CHOICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Choice means of very good quality, and also a selection.

clue.text: Greek character stops behind raised weapon

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted up means read bottom to top
plugs a gap, so it sits inside

explanation.surface: A Greek hero halts after lifting his sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a figure from Greek myth; it is a letter of the alphabet. 'Stops' is the verb for plugging a hole, as with a stopper.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapier is a slender thrusting sword.

clue.text: Strange article about invention

indicators.note: goes round the next piece

parts.note: a lie is an invention, a made-up story

explanation.surface: An odd piece of writing concerning a new gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' reads as a newspaper piece and 'invention' as a gadget; they are AN and LIE. A(LIE)N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the adjective sense: something foreign to your experience feels strange.

clue.text: Successor man announced in letter?

definitions.note: airmail is a way of sending a letter, so the question mark marks the definition by example

indicators.note: said out loud, so the sound counts

parts.note: an heir is a successor, male = man

explanation.surface: A letter announces who will inherit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that airmail is one kind of letter, not a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: a letter flown overseas is sent by this service.

clue.text: Genuine monarch's principal possession?

indicators.note: the chief letter of a word is its first

explanation.surface: A king's most prized true possession.
explanation.walkthrough: A monarch's chief possession is the kingdom itself, which is why 'possession' gets a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom, the territory a monarch holds.

clue.text: Cut into network cable at both ends

indicators.note: take just the first and last letters

explanation.surface: An engineer slices into network cabling at each end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut into' is a verb and the definition, not a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To lance is to cut into, as a surgeon lances a boil.

clue.text: Judgement voided debatable conclusion

indicators.note: emptied, so only the outer letters remain

explanation.surface: A ruling has thrown out a contested finding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voided' sounds legal, like a judgement being overturned; it means emptying a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal sense: a court's formal decision on a disputed point is called this, the same as its judgement.

clue.text: Sign up loner to go travelling

indicators.note: the letters set off and move around

explanation.surface: A solitary type joins a group tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' belongs to the definition, sign up, not a reversal instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: putting your name down for a course or club, the British spelling with one L.

clue.text: Fantastic story can spread in capital city

indicators.note: placed in the next word, so it sits between that word's letters
the letters are spread out and rearranged

explanation.surface: A tall tale that a tin can was smeared around the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, as in 'the story can spread'; it is the noun, a tin, supplying three letters to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A romance is a fanciful tale of adventure, originally a medieval tale of chivalry.
